title: First Drive: Bugatti's Bolide Hypercar Is a Meteoric Machine on Miami's F1 Circuit
excerpt: We test-drove the Bugatti Bolide on Miami’s Formula 1 circuit, where the hypercar stays glued to the track—despite rainy conditions.
content:
“It’s just a car,” Bugatti’s head driving instructor tells me, repeating the reminder a few times as I stand beside the marque’s $4.8 million Bolide. The assurance comes at the end of a briefing rife with warnings before I drive the limited-edition model around the Miami International Autodrome, home to the city’s eponymous Formula 1 grand prix. “Actually, it’s a gun,” he adds with a smirk. “But it’s just a car.”

With a name that fittingly means fireball or meteor, the track-only Bolide is the most extreme machine Bugatti has ever built. Only 40 have been made—all delivered—and each is powered by the automaker’s 8.0-liter quad-turbocharged W16. That engine’s output is 1,578 hp and 1,180 ft lbs of torque on standard gas. (Those figures jump to 1,826 hp and 1,475 ft lbs of torque with race fuel.)

A handful of owners are also on hand to test-fire their ballistic examples for the first time. Spotting even one Bolide in the wild is incredibly rare; seeing a pack of them hurtling down the circuit’s main straight induces goose bumps. I contort my tall frame into the passenger side of the carbon-fiber-monocoque car’s cockpit, sitting beside Le Mans winner Andy Wallace, Bugatti’s chief test-driver, who is about to acquaint me with the course. Then the sky darkens and unleashes torrents of rain. Wallace explains that the Bolide handles wonderfully in the wet. Easy for him to say.

Once the storm passes, we’re off. Within seconds, he’s matted the accelerator. “Get on the brakes early and much harder than you think,” Wallace yells over the engine as we accelerate north of 200 mph. He demonstrates by stomping on the brake pedal, slamming me into my six-point harness.

The Bolide’s brakes are the talk of the paddock, and for good reason. Brembo spent two years developing the largest carbon-carbon brake system it has ever made, a setup similar to those used on the Concorde and in Formula 1. The result: The Bolide generates braking forces of up to −2.5 G.

When it’s my turn in the driver’s seat, I’m first struck by the surprising amount of visibility through the windshield. My gaze shifts to the X-shape steering wheel, which echoes the design motif of the rear fascia and spoiler. Then there’s the soundtrack. As marvelous as the sonic signature is from the outside, it’s something else entirely within the cockpit: an intoxicating rumble and whine.

Bury your foot and trust the car. Under full acceleration, the sensation is nearly overwhelming. Within a few blinks, the red-and-white curbing blurs into a solid pink, and a hint of tunnel vision creeps in while the electronic stability control steadies the Bolide. Yet I feel no resistance (or assistance, for that matter) from the chassis. Nothing is fighting me. This car always feels planted, glued to the track, thanks in large part to the aero package capable of generating more than 6,000 pounds of downforce—double that of a Formula 1 racer at speed.

The W16, with its layered howl of turbos and combustion, sits close enough behind your shoulders that you feel it as much as hear it—a life-affirming vibration through the seat and into your chest at full rip. What is genuinely remarkable, though, is that this meteoric machine drives with the straightforwardness of a Toyota Camry. All the apprehension I’d carried into the day dissolved somewhere around turn six. After all, it’s just a car. But a $4.8 million car that only 40 people in the world can call their own.
